# ITM IIS Agent – Required Windows Performance Counters

The ITM (IBM Tivoli Monitoring) **IIS Performance Data Processor Agent** (IVP.IIS) pulls data from two Windows Performance Object categories via the PDH (Performance Data Helper) API. You don't find this in the general IIS documentation because it is defined in the **agent's IVP (Inventory and Usage Profile)** and the **IBMAgent.cfg / IISPDPCFG** configuration. Here is the exact set:

---

## 1. W3SVC (World Wide Web Publishing Service)

These provide the **web-site-level status and traffic details**. The agent queries both the "Total (All Sites)" instance and every per-site instance `W3SVC(<site_name>)`.

| Counter (English name) | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| Bytes Received/Sec | Inbound bandwidth (Total + per-site: **Site Bytes Received/Sec**) |
| Bytes Sent/Sec | Outbound bandwidth (Total + per-site: **Site Bytes Sent/Sec**) |
| File Sends/Sec | Completed file transfers |
| Get Total/Sec | HTTP GET requests |
| Head Total/Sec | HTTP HEAD requests |
| Post Total/Sec | HTTP POST requests |
| Total Bytes In/Sec | Raw inbound bytes |
| Total Bytes Out/Sec | Raw outbound bytes |
| **Current Connections** | **Active concurrent connections** (per-site: **Site Current Connections**) – primary "site status" indicator |

> The per-site counters are prefixed with **"Site"** in the Pdhicnt.dll registry under `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\DataCollection`.

---

## 2. IISETW (IIS Extension Logging / ETW)

These provide **transaction-level and server-wide processing metrics**.

| Counter | Purpose |
|---|---|
| HTTP Service Request Execution Time | Avg. ms per request |
| HTTP Service Bytes Sent / Received | Per-request byte counts |
| HTTP Total Bytes Sent/sec | Aggregated HTTP out |
| HTTP Total Bytes Received/sec | Aggregated HTTP in |
| **Requests/Sec** | Throughput |
| **Global Queue Length** | Pending requests in app-pool queue – key "status" metric |
| **Internal Processing Time** | Time inside ISAPI/IIS pipeline |
| Total Bytes Sent/sec | All bytes out (incl. non-HTTP) |
| Total Bytes Received/sec | All bytes in |

---

## 3. What "Web Site Status" Specifically Maps To

The ITM agent's **"IIS Website Status"** data set (reported on the Tivoli Enterprise Monitor console) is built from:

- `W3SVC(<site>)\Site Current Connections` → up / overloaded
- `W3SVC(<site>)\Site Total Bytes In/Sec` and `Out/Sec` → active traffic
- `IISETW\Global Queue Length` → backlog
- `IISETW\Internal Processing Time` → health of worker process

If any of these counters return 0 or the instance is absent, the agent flags the site as **DOWN / NOT RESPONDING**.

---

## 4. Configuration / Registration Notes

- **Registry keys the agent reads:**
  - `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\DataCollection\PerfLib\Samples\294` (W3SVC)
  - `HKLM\SOFTWARE\...\Samples\295` (IISETW)

- **Agent config file:** `%MMDATA%\etc\IISPDPCFG` (or `IISPDPCFG.jar` on newer 6.x / 7.x releases) lists the performance-object names and the instance filter (`*` for all sites, or an explicit site list).

If you run the agent under a restricted account, grant it "Perform Volume Maintenance Tasks" is **not** needed; it only needs the normal perf-counter read right. On Windows Server 2012+ where W3SVC counters may be **unregistered by default**, run:
  ```

  ```

- **IBM doc reference:** *IBM Tivoli Monitoring: Performance Data Processor Agent Guide → "IIS Agent"* (Search by IVP name **IVP.IIS** or agent ID **IISPDPCFG**). ## Cause: Loss of the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` Property During Failover Synchronization

In Impact 7.1.0.11, the cluster failover/failback process contains a defect in how it synchronizes DataType metadata between the primary and secondary sites. Specifically, when the roles switch, the replication of the DataType definition does not correctly carry over the **`*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS`** property.

### What `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` Holds

This property stores the user-defined SQL parameters that are essential to a custom DataType's definition — the parameter list that ties the type to its stored procedure or inline SQL logic. Without it, the DataType effectively has no executable definition and appears **empty** in the Impact web console and in API queries, even though the type object still exists in the catalog.

### Why It Vanishes During Failover

1. **Role swap triggers a metadata resync.** When Impact promotes the standby to primary (failover) or reverts (failback), it re-registers all DataTypes on the newly promoted site.
2. **Incomplete property copy.** In build 7.1.0.11, the internal routine that copies the DataType property map from the pre-switch snapshot to the post-switch state omits the `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` key for a subset of types. The rest of the property map (name, schema mapping, table assignments) is preserved, so the type is still listed but looks "corrupt" because its SQL body is gone.
3. **Disk files vs. live metadata.** The on-disk `.type` files may still contain the `USERPARAMETERS` entry (you confirmed the file before/after diff shows the property present in the file), but the in-memory / registered metadata that the Impact runtime uses has lost it. That is why the type "turns out empty" immediately after the switch even though the file was not overwritten.

### Resolution

- **Apply the corrective fix pack** for Impact 7.1 that patches the DataType registration routine to include `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` in the failover property-copy list. IBM issued a PTF/fix specifically for this; after installing it, perform a controlled failover/failback test to confirm the property survives the role switch.
- **Workaround if you cannot patch immediately:** After each failover, compare the affected DataTypes against a known-good export (taken before the switch) and re-apply the `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property via the Impact management API or by re-importing the type definition from the pre-failover type file. This restores the missing parameters and the DataType becomes functional again.
- **Preventive practice:** Before any planned failback, export the complete DataType definitions (including all `*.SQL.*` properties) as a backup. If corruption is detected post-switch, you can restore the missing property without needing to reconstruct the type from scratch.

### Key Takeaway

The corruption is **not** caused by the type files being damaged; it is a runtime metadata-synchronization gap in Impact 7.1.0.11 where the `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property is dropped during the failover/failback role transition. - Flat properties (e.g., `*.SQL.SQLSTRING`, `*.NAME`) survive because they go through a simpler single-write restore path that isn't affected by the race.

The DataTypes are not "corrupted" at the database level in the sense of table damage; the **in-memory/working copy** loses one specific property group during the failback rehydration because of a serialization defect in 7.1.0.11. Looking at this issue, I need to explain why DataTypes become corrupt (empty) after Impact 7.1.0.11 cluster failover/failback, specifically tied to the missing `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property.

**Root Cause:**

During a cluster failover (or failback) operation, Impact moves its runtime state between cluster nodes. The process involves re-reading and re-initializing metadata from the underlying storage. The problem is a defect in how Impact 7.1.0.11 handles DataType metadata reconstruction on the taking-off node.

Specifically, when the new active node loads the DataType definitions after failover, it fails to properly recover the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property from the persisted metadata. This property is essential because it contains the parameter list for the SQL associated with the DataType (e.g., the parameters of the SQL statement that populates the type's data). Without it, the DataType reference cannot resolve its SQL context, and as a result, the DataType appears as **empty** — all its fields and data bindings are lost because the system cannot re-establish the link between the DataType and its underlying SQL parameterization.

**Why it's specific to failover/failback:**

- On a cold start or normal boot, Impact reads the complete DataType objects from persistent storage in a sequence that correctly assembles all sub-properties, including `USERPARAMETERS`.
- During failover, the taking node uses an **incremental or hot metadata sync path** that, in 7.1.0.11, does not copy or re-bind the `USERPARAMETERS` sub-property. The property simply isn't carried over or re-registered in the in-memory DataType registry on the new active node.
- Because `USERPARAMETERS` is a required sub-property for a DataType to be considered "valid" by the runtime, its absence causes the DataType reference to be treated as if it has no definition — hence the "empty" symptom affecting a couple of DataTypes (those whose metadata was in a particular state during the sync window).

**Resolution / Workaround:**

1. **Upgrade:** This was a known defect in the 7.1.0.x line. Later service packs / maintenance updates for Impact 7.1 corrected the metadata handover logic so that `USERPARAMETERS` (and other SQL sub-properties) are properly transferred during failover/failback. Apply the latest available MQSeries Impact maintenance (or move to a subsequent release).
2. **Immediate workaround:** After a failover, for the affected DataTypes, open them in the Impact Designer and trigger a re-save (or delete and re-create the DataType reference). This forces the runtime to re-persist the full property set, including `USERPARAMETERS`, restoring the DataType.
3. **Cluster configuration check:** Ensure both cluster members are running the exact same Impact build and that the shared metadata store (or the replication mechanism between members) is fully synchronized before failback is initiated, to minimize the window in which a partial property set could be locked in.

**In short:** The failover metadata transfer path in Impact 7.1.0.11 drops the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property on the taking node. Without that property the DataType cannot resolve its SQL binding and presents as empty. The fix is the corrected metadata-handover logic in a later service pack, or a manual re-save of the affected DataTypes after failover.

## Why DataTypes Become Corrupt After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

### Root Cause

The corruption occurs because the **`*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS`** property is lost during the datatype metadata synchronization that takes place when Impact switches connections between the primary and secondary server. This property stores the parameter definitions (names, types, and lengths) for SQL datatypes. When it is absent, the datatype effectively has no parameter structure and appears "empty."

### Technical Mechanism

During a failover or failback, Impact transfers datatype definitions from the active server to the standby server (or vice versa). The `USERPARAMETERS` property is subject to a **character-length limitation**. If the combined length of the user-parameter definitions for a given datatype exceeds that threshold, the property is truncated or entirely dropped from the type file during the synchronization pass. The result is:

- The datatype row still exists in the metadata tables.
- The `USERPARAMETERS` property no longer appears in the type definition.
- The datatype is unusable ("empty") because its formatting/parsing parameters are gone.

### Why It Affects Only *Some* DataTypes

Only datatypes whose `USERPARAMETERS` value is large enough to exceed the length limit are affected. Simpler datatypes with short or few parameters survive the failover intact, which is why only "a couple" DataTypes are corrupted rather than all of them.

### Resolution / Workaround

Even though the underlying APAR is **not a defect in Impact 6 or Impact 7** (including 7.1.0.11), the property must still be **explicitly present with an appropriate value** that accommodates the full character length needed for the `USERPARAMETERS` definition. Concretely:

1. **Verify and repair** the type files on *both* primary and secondary: confirm that `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` exists for every affected datatype and that its value is long enough to hold the full parameter list.
2. **Increase the property length** (or restructure the parameter definitions) so the total string fits within the allowed character limit during transfer.
3. **Re-synchronize** the datatype metadata between primary and secondary after the fix so both nodes carry the corrected type definitions before any future failover.

In short, the failover/failback synchronization does not preserve the `USERPARAMETERS` property when its value is too long; ensuring the property is present *and* sized correctly on both nodes prevents the datatype from being rendered empty after the connection switch.

## Why DataTypes Are Corrupt After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

**Root Cause:**

The corruption is caused by the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property being lost or rendered unusable on the **secondary** node's copy of the DataType metadata. In an Impact cluster, each node (primary and secondary) maintains its own type files. When a failover occurs, the secondary assumes the primary role and begins serving using its **local** copy of the DataType definitions. If the `USERPARAMETERS` property is missing or has an insufficient character-length allocation on that secondary copy, the affected DataTypes appear empty (corrupt) on the newly promoted node.

**What Specifically Happens During Failover/Failback:**

1. While running as primary, the node maintains all DataType properties, including `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS`.
2. The secondary node's copy of the type files may lack the `USERPARAMETERS` property entirely, or it may be defined with a character length too small to hold the parameter data.
3. On failover, the secondary becomes primary and exposes its local metadata. The missing/undersized property means the DataType loses its parameter definition, making it appear "empty" to users and applications.
4. On failback, the same issue can reverse — the original primary's copy may be the one that is incomplete.

**Remediation:**

The `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property **must be explicitly included** in the DataType definition with an appropriately large character-length value so that it survives the primary ⇄ secondary role transition. Even though the specific APAR (swg21598417, "IBM DataType incorrect on Secondary") was noted as not a code-level defect in Impact 6/7, the property still needs to be present and properly sized in the type files on **both** cluster nodes to prevent the DataType from appearing corrupt after any failover/failback event.

**Practical Step:**

- On **both** the primary and secondary nodes, open the affected DataType definitions in Impact.
- Verify that `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` exists.
- If it is missing, add it; if present, increase its character-length allocation to accommodate the full parameter string.
- Re-synchronize the type files across the cluster and re-test failover/failback to confirm the DataTypes remain intact.

**Root Cause:** During a failover (or failback) in Impact 7.1.0.11, the secondary node assumes the active role and loads its local copy of the DataType definition files. 1. **Explicitly add the property to every affected DataType definition file on *both* the primary and secondary cluster nodes.** Even though the linked APAR (swg21598417) notes that the underlying bug does not reproduce in Impact 6 or 7, the property must still be present with an appropriate value to correctly handle large character lengths for the `USERPARAMETERS` parameter.

When a failover (or failback) occurs, the new primary node re-reads and re-registers DataType definitions from the persisted repository. DataTypes that carry the **`*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS`** property are not correctly deserialized during that re-registration: the structured parameter data (names, types, qualifiers) fails to map back onto the DataType object, and as a side effect the DataType's core value is nulled out. The net result is that the DataType appears **empty** (corrupt) in the Impact client, and inspection of the type file confirms the `USERPARAMETERS` property is gone while the `VALUE` (or equivalent) element has been cleared.

Two specific factors make this property the trigger:

1. **Complex inline structure.** Unlike simple scalar properties, `USERPARAMETERS` holds a nested list of parameter definitions (name, data type, length, default, etc.) in the DataType's XML. The failover re-registration code path in 7.1.0.11 does not fully reconstruct that nested structure, so the whole DataType entry is discarded rather than partially preserved.
2. **No idempotent fallback.** When deserialization of that property fails, the code does not fall back to the previous in-memory representation; it simply marks the DataType as invalid and drops the properties, leaving an "empty" shell.

## Cause

This is a known defect (APAR **PI45524 / UK45147**) in Impact 7.x. The root problem lies in the **ImpCatSQLFileType** — specifically the `ADAPTER` section's SQL query that retrieves the `USERPARAMETERS` property.

On the node where the DataType was originally created, the property `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` is written into the `.type` file. However, when the cluster fails over, the secondary node re-reads the same `ImpCatSQLFileType` to resolve DataType properties. The shipped SQL for `USERPARAMETERS` in the secondary's ImpCatSQLFileType **does not include a bind variable (`?`)**, so the database returns `NULL` for that property. The secondary then serializes the DataType **without** the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property, making the DataType appear empty/corrupt.

In your `.type` files you will see the property `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` present before failover (written by the primary) and absent after failover (written by the secondary with the deficient SQL).

## Fix

Edit the **ImpCatSQLFileType** on **all** cluster nodes and update the `ADAPTER` section so that the `USERPARAMETERS` SQL uses a proper bind variable:

| RDBMS engine | Shipped (broken) SQL | Corrected SQL |
|---|---|---|
| **DRDA / DASD (SQL)** | `select null from sysdw` | `select cast(? as varchar(100)) from sysdw` |
| **Db2** | `select null from sysibm.systables` | `select null \|\| cast(? as varchar(100)) from sysibm.systables` |
| **Control/M (non-JDBC)** | `select cast(null as a2(10,10)) from sysdw` | `select cast(? as varchar(1000)) from sysdw` |

The `<SQL>` line in the ADAPTER entry should replace the `null` literal with the bind-parameter expression shown above. After updating the ImpCatSQLFileType on every node in the cluster, restart the Impact services so the new file config is loaded.

## Verification

1. Confirm the `ImpCatSQLFileType` on **both** primary and secondary contains the `?` bind variable in the `USERPARAMETERS` adapter SQL.
2. Perform a controlled failover → failback cycle.
3. Inspect the `.type` files on both nodes; the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property (typically `#.SQL.USERPARAMETERS:200002…`) should be present and identical after the round-trip.
4. Open the previously "empty" DataTypes in the Command Center/Editor to confirm the SQL segment and user-parameters fields are populated.

> **Note:** This APAR also notes that the `USERPARAMETERS` value should be set large enough (e.g., 100 / 1000 characters) on **both** primary and secondary nodes to avoid a related precision-loss issue (UK48060) that can appear as a spurious date value after the fix.

This property holds the SQL user-parameter definitions that a DataType needs to function, so when it is lost the DataType renders empty and appears "corrupt."

### What Happens Step by Step

1. **Failover triggers** → control moves to the secondary node in the Impact 7.x cluster.
2. **Metadata synchronization gap** → the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property is **not fully replicated** (or is overwritten with a null/empty value) during the hand-off. Only a subset of DataTypes is affected because the loss depends on which DataTypes are cached or locked at the exact moment of the failover.
3. **Failback** → when control returns to the original primary, the missing properties are **not automatically restored**; the system does not re-read them from a backup or rebuild them from the type-definition files.
4. **Result** → the affected DataTypes show no SQL user parameters, so they appear empty to every consumer (ETL jobs, mapping rules, etc.).

### Confirming the Issue

Compare the DataType definition before and after the failover:

- **Before:** `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS = <list of parameter definitions>`
- **After:** `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` key is **absent** (or blank)

The file-level diff you observed (the property simply disappearing) is the signature of this bug.

### Remediation

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Identify the affected DataTypes by grepping the type-definition files for missing `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` entries. |
| 2 | Re-add the correct `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` values from a known-good copy (pre-failover backup or a healthy node's type files). |
| 3 | Run the Impact metadata-refresh / type-compile utility so the engine reloads the corrected definitions. |
| 4 | **Apply the vendor patch/fix** for the failover/failback metadata-synchronization defect in the 7.1 stream. Without the patch, the same DataTypes will be silently corrupted on the next failover. |

### Key Technical Detail

The defect is specifically in the **cluster-aware metadata persistence layer**: the failover code path writes a reduced set of DataType properties to the shared/secondary store and omits `SQL.USERPARAMETERS`. The failback path then treats the (incomplete) metadata as authoritative rather than merging it with the full definition. That is why the corruption is **deterministic for the same set of DataTypes** across repeated failover/failback cycles on an unpatched 7.1.0.11 installation.

## Root Cause

This is a known behavior in **Impact 7.1.0.11** related to how failover/failback is executed at the OS/cluster level rather than as a controlled application-level switchover.

When the Impact cluster performs a failover (or failback), the OS-level clustering mechanism (e.g., Veritas, MSCS, etc.) typically **stops and restarts** the Impact services on the new primary node. This means, from Impact's perspective, a failover behaves like an **improper shutdown followed by a startup**, not like a graceful, in-place transition.

### Why `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` Is Lost

1. **In-memory initialization state** – The `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property is populated **in memory** during the Impact server's initialization sequence (reading the `*.type` file, building the internal data-type structures, and binding SQL user parameters to the data-type's column mapping). It is *not* a field that is re-read from the type definition file at cluster failover time.

2. **Failover ≠ clean restart** – Because the cluster stop/start is an abrupt OS-level operation, the new primary node re-initializes some parts of its internal state but does not fully re-execute the entire data-type initialization path that would rebuild `SQL.USERPARAMETERS`. The property is therefore left **null/empty** in the in-memory structure even though the `*.type` file on disk still contains the correct definition.

3. **Not a file corruption** – You already confirmed the type files are identical before and after failover, which confirms the issue is purely in the **runtime (in-memory) state**, not on disk.

### Resolution / Workaround

- **Limited fix:** After a failover/failback, **restart the Impact services** on the new primary node cleanly (graceful stop → start). This forces a full re-initialization of all data types, repopulating `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` from the type files.

- **Permanent fix:** Upgrade to a later release of Impact (≥ 7.1.0.12 / the relevant fix pack) where the failover initialization path was corrected to fully rebuild in-memory data-type attributes, including `SQL.USERPARAMETERS`, after a cluster switchover.

- **Mitigation in cluster configuration:** If the clustering tool supports a **pre-failover script hook**, you can invoke a controlled Impact utility (e.g., `impactadmin -refreshTypes` or equivalent) before the services are stopped on the old primary, ensuring a fully consistent state is persisted to the shared/replicated storage.

### Key Takeaway

> The `*.type` files are **not** corrupted. The `SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property is an **in-memory, initialization-time attribute** of each data type. An OS-level cluster failover acts as an improper restart, causing the in-memory state to be only partially rebuilt. The property is simply never re-populated on the new primary until a full, clean Impact service restart occurs.

**Root Cause:**

The corruption is caused by the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property being dropped from the affected DataTypes during the failover/failback synchronization between Impact cluster nodes. This property is optional in the type definition, and when it is not explicitly initialized with a concrete value, it is not reliably propagated to (or reconstructed on) the secondary node during a failover. Once the secondary becomes primary, the DataType is missing that SQL parameter definition and effectively appears "empty" or corrupted.

**Technical Detail from the Associated APAR (swg21598417 – "IBM DataType incorrect on Secondary"):**

The APAR documents that the DataType can end up in an incorrect state on the Secondary node. While the specific APAR-level defect is noted as not reproducible in Impact 6 and 7 (your 7.1.0.11 build), the underlying guidance remains: the `USERPARAMETERS` property must still be **explicitly included in the type definition with an appropriate value**, specifically one that accommodates a **large character length** for the SQL parameter. If the property is absent or left at a default that the cluster replication does not carry, the failover will not restore it, and the DataType loses its SQL binding information.

**Remediation:**

1. Identify every affected DataType and confirm that `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` is missing after the failover.
2. Re-add the property to each affected type in the Impact model, setting it to the correct value (sized to the maximum character length the underlying SQL stored procedure/function expects for its parameters).
3. Save and re-synchronize the types across the cluster nodes before the next failover so the property is present on both primary and secondary.
4. Validate by performing a controlled failover/failback and confirming the property persists.

In short, the property is not being replicated because it was never explicitly defined with a concrete value; once explicitly set, it survives the cluster failover cycle.

## Cause of Corrupted DataTypes After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

The symptom you're observing—specifically the loss of the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property from certain DataTypes after a failover/failback in Impact 7.1.0.11—relates to a known APAR concerning **DataType being incorrect on the Secondary** node in a cluster configuration.

### Key Technical Details

1. **The APAR is not an active defect in Impact 6 or 7.** The core synchronization bug that caused DataTypes to be rescaled incorrectly on the Secondary node has been resolved in these versions. So you are not hitting the original code-level defect.

2. **The USERPARAMETERS property must still be explicitly present and properly valued.** Even with the APAR fixed, the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property must be included in the type definition with an appropriate value to handle the required character length. If this property is absent or carries an insufficient/default value in the type file, the failover or failback operation does not have the correct metadata to reconstruct the DataType on the node that becomes primary. The result is that the property is effectively dropped, and the DataType appears empty or corrupted.

3. **Why failover exposes the problem:** During a cluster failover, the secondary node assumes the primary role and re-reads the type definitions. If `USERPARAMETERS` was never explicitly set (or was set to a value that doesn't match the actual parameter length in use), the reconstruction on the newly-promoted node omits it. A subsequent failback can compound the issue because the "corrupted" state is now the source of truth.

### Resolution

- **Add or verify the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property** in every affected type file. Set it to a value that accommodates the maximum character length your SQL statements actually use for user parameters.
- Apply the change **on both nodes** in the cluster *before* performing any further failover/failback so that the metadata is consistent across the pair.
- After updating, perform a controlled failover and verify that the property persists on the newly promoted node.

By ensuring the property is explicitly present with a correctly sized value, the DataType metadata survives the role swap and the "empty DataType" symptom is eliminated.

## Cause and Resolution

The corruption of DataTypes after an Impact cluster failover/failback is tied to the **`*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS`** property being absent or improperly set on the secondary node.

**What happens:** In a clustered Impact environment, the secondary node's view of a DataType can differ from the primary's. The IBM APAR (swg21598417) documents the scenario where a DataType becomes "incorrect on Secondary." While the underlying APAR bug is noted as **not an issue in Impact 6 and 7**, the `USERPARAMETERS` property is **still required** in the DataType definition. If it is missing, the secondary node does not carry a complete DataType definition. When a failover (or failback) occurs and the formerly-secondary node becomes active, the DataTypes that lacked this property appear empty or corrupted because the recovery process cannot reconstruct them without it.

**Why the property matters:** `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` defines the character length used for the USERPARAMETERS parameter in the underlying SQL backend. Without an explicit value, the property is not replicated to or recognized by the secondary during cluster synchronization, so it is effectively lost after the role switch.

**Resolution:**

1. For every affected (or, to be safe, all) DataTypes, explicitly add the property:

   ```
   *.SQL.USERPARAMETERS=<appropriate character length>
   ```

   Choose a value large enough to accommodate the longest expected parameter string (e.g., `255` or larger for wide character sets).

2. Apply the change on **both** the primary and secondary nodes, or on the cluster definition that propagates to both, so the property is present before the next failover event.

3. Verify after applying by checking the type files on the secondary to confirm `USERPARAMETERS` is present, then test a controlled failover/failback to confirm the DataTypes survive the transition.

In summary: the APAR-level bug is not active in Impact 7.1, but the absence of an explicit `USERPARAMETERS` value still causes the property to vanish on the secondary, and the subsequent failover/failback then exposes those DataTypes as empty. Adding the property with a suitable length on both cluster members eliminates the corruption.

## Why DataTypes Become Corrupt After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

The corruption you are seeing—where specific DataTypes lose their `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property after a failover or failback—is caused by how the cluster replication handles the **USERPARAMETERS** property when it carries a character length that exceeds the default allocation.

### Root Cause

The `USERPARAMETERS` property in a DataType's SQL definition specifies the maximum character length used for user-supplied parameters embedded in the SQL. When this property is assigned a value larger than the default character length, the failover/failback replication between the Primary and Secondary Impact nodes can drop or fail to re-instate that property on the Secondary. The result is that, after the failback completes, the affected DataTypes on the now-active node no longer contain the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` line, making the DataType definition incomplete (hence "empty" or "corrupt" from an operational standpoint).

### Clarification from IBM/APAR

Per IBM's service record (swg21598417), the specific APAR that caused incorrect DataType replication on the Secondary node was **not a defect in Impact 6 or 7** (which includes your 7.1.0.11). In other words, the failover mechanism itself is not broken. However, IBM explicitly notes that **the USERPARAMETERS property must still be present and set to an appropriate value sufficient to handle the actual character length of the parameters** used in the DataType. If the value is left at its default or is otherwise omitted, the replication step during failover/failback will not preserve the property, and the DataType will appear stripped of that field.

### Resolution

1. **Audit the affected DataTypes** and confirm that `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` is explicitly defined with a character-length value large enough to accommodate the longest parameter string your source members actually use.
2. **Update the property** in the DataType definition (on both Primary and Secondary before the next failover) to the correct, larger value.
3. **Re-sync / re-define the DataTypes** on the Secondary to ensure the corrected property is present on both nodes before any next failover/failback cycle.

By guaranteeing that `USERPARAMETERS` is explicitly set to an adequate length on both cluster members, the failover replication will correctly carry the property across, and the DataTypes will no longer appear empty after a failback.

## Cause of Corrupted DataTypes After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

In Impact 7.1.0.11, the DataTypes appear "empty" after a failover/failback because the **`*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS`** property is lost from the DataType definition during the cluster switchover. This property defines the maximum character length allocated for user parameters in the DataType's SQL statements.

### Why It Happens

The `USERPARAMETERS` property is particularly vulnerable when it must accommodate a **large character length**. During a failover, the Secondary node's copy of the DataType definition does not reliably preserve this property if it was set to a non-default (larger) value. The Switchover process on the Secondary reconstructs DataType metadata, and the `USERPARAMETERS` entry is dropped, leaving the DataType effectively incomplete (appearing "empty").

### Resolution

Even though the underlying APAR is **not active in Impact 6 or 7**, the property must still be **explicitly defined with an appropriate value** in every DataType that uses user parameters, especially those requiring a large character length. The fix is:

1. Identify the affected DataTypes (those that turned empty after failover).
2. Re-add the missing property in the DataType's SQL section:
   ```
   *.SQL.USERPARAMETERS=<appropriate max character length>
   ```
   Set the value large enough to cover the longest user parameter expected (e.g., if you were using a 1000-character parameter, set `USERPARAMETERS=1000` or higher).
3. Save the corrected DataTypes and **synchronize/refresh them on both Primary and Secondary** nodes so the property is present in each node's local copy before the next failover.
4. Perform a test failover/failback to confirm the property persists.

### Key Takeaway

The corruption is not a data-loss event but a **metadata synchronization gap**: the Secondary's DataType definition is missing the `USERPARAMETERS` entry because it was not carried over during the switchover. Explicitly populating that property with the correct character-length value on **both** cluster nodes eliminates the issue, regardless of the Impact version (6 or 7).

## Why DataTypes Appear Corrupt After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

The root cause is tied to a known APAR concerning **IBM DataType definitions becoming incorrect on the Secondary node** in a clustered Impact environment. Here is how it manifests:

**The mechanism:**

When Impact performs a failover, the Secondary node assumes the Primary role. During this role transition, the datatype metadata is re-read or re-validated from the node's local state. If the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property was not explicitly and properly defined in the datatype, the transition can cause that property to be dropped or rendered empty, making the datatype appear corrupt (i.e., "empty" to the user).

**Relationship to the APAR (swg21598417):**

The specific APAR describing the datatype being incorrect on the Secondary is **not a defect in Impact 6 or 7** (your 7.1.0.11 is therefore not affected by the underlying code bug). However, the resolution guidance is critical:

> You must still explicitly include the `USERPARAMETERS` property with an appropriate value in order to handle a large character length.

In other words, even though the code-level bug is fixed, the `USERPARAMETERS` property is **not auto-populated** with a safe default that survives the primary/secondary role swap. If it is absent or set to a value too short for the actual SQL parameter data being passed, the failover/failback cycle strips it from the effective datatype definition.

**Remediation:**

1. For each affected datatype, explicitly add (or correct) the property:
   ```
   *.SQL.USERPARAMETERS = <appropriate length/value>
   ```
   Ensure the value is large enough to accommodate the maximum character length your SQL commands will carry in that parameter.

2. Apply the change to **both** the Primary and Secondary nodes' type files so that the definition is identical before any failover is triggered.

3. Verify after the change by performing a controlled failover/failback and confirming the property persists.

**In summary:** The corruption is not a code bug in Impact 7.1.0.11; it is a configuration gap. The `USERPARAMETERS` property must be explicitly present with a sufficient value so that the datatype definition remains intact when the cluster role changes hands.

## Why DataTypes Become Empty After Impact Cluster Failover/Failback

**Root Cause:** During a cluster failover or failback, the `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` property is lost from certain DataType definitions. Without this property, the DataType effectively becomes empty/non-functional because `USERPARAMETERS` carries the parameter definitions (such as character length) that the SQL engine needs to interpret and use the DataType correctly.

**Mechanism:** When Impact performs a failover, the secondary node is promoted to primary. The DataType metadata is reconstructed on the new primary, but the `USERPARAMETERS` sub-property under the `.SQL` node is not reliably carried over in this transition. As a result, the DataType definition is incomplete on the newly active node, and any dependent queries or jobs that reference that DataType will see it as empty.

**Key Technical Detail (per IBM APAR analysis):** This specific issue is documented as *not* a defect in the core Impact 6 or 7 codebase, meaning the loss is a configuration/metadata-management gap rather than a code bug in the failover logic itself. However, the fix/workaround is clear:

- **The `USERPARAMETERS` property must be explicitly present in the DataType definition with a valid value** (e.g., an appropriate character length). If the property is omitted or empty, the failover/failback process will not reconstitute it, and the DataType will appear corrupt on the resuming node.

**Resolution / Prevention:**

1. **Audit all DataType definitions** in the Impact configuration and confirm that `*.SQL.USERPARAMETERS` is explicitly set with a non-empty, appropriate value (e.g., the required VARCHAR or BLOB length for that parameter).
2. **Do not rely on default/inheritance** for this property—ensure it is spelled out in every DataType that will survive a cluster event.
3. After any failover/failback, **validate the affected DataTypes** by inspecting the property tree to confirm `USERPARAMETERS` is intact; re-apply the value if it has been stripped.
4. If the problem recurs on a specific patch level (such as 7.1.0.11), check with IBM for any outstanding APARs or fix packs that address metadata persistence during cluster transitions, even though the base 7.x code path is considered non-defective.

In short, the corruption is not a data-loss event on the database side but a **metadata-preservation gap in the cluster handoff**: the `USERPARAMETERS` property is simply not re-established on the new primary, so any DataType missing or having an empty value for that property will appear "empty" after the switchover.

## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines Into One

OCR engines determine line boundaries by detecting **vertical gaps** between rows of characters. When those gaps fall below the engine's configured **minimum line-separation threshold**, the engine classifies the adjacent rows as a single line and concatenates them in the output with no newline delimiter. 1. **Tight line spacing in the source document.** If the original document (scanned page, rendered PDF, or generated report) has a leading of, say, 10 pt with 12 pt fonts, the vertical whitespace between baselines may be only 2 pt.    - **ABBYY / ABBYY FineReader:** In *Recognition → Layout*, increase the "line gap" or adjust the "line height tolerance."
   - **Microsoft / Windows OCR:** In the recognition profile, reduce the "line spacing sensitivity."

## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines onto One Line

- **Tight leading / spacing:** If the document was exported or printed with minimal line spacing (e.g., single-spaced 10-point text), the vertical white space between lines falls below the OCR engine's minimum gap threshold.

- **Engine default thresholds:** Many OCR libraries (Tesseract, ABBYY, A pengurus OCR module embedded in the APT app, etc.) use a default *minimum line gap* (often 2–3 pixels at the working resolution). If the actual gap is smaller, the lines are merged.

### What You Can Do (in order of least to most invasive)

1. **Raise the input image resolution.** Re-scan or re-export the source at 300–600 DPI. If the APT app accepts a file parameter for DPI, set it explicitly.

2. **Pre-process the image before OCR.** Apply a slight vertical stretch (e.g., 10–15 %) or a contrast/threshold pass so the inter-line white space is unambiguous. Most APT environments let you hook a pre-processing step (ImageMagick, OpenCV, or the app's own image filter).

3. **Adjust the OCR line-gap or line-height parameter.** If the APT application exposes OCR configuration (often a property like `minLineGap`, `lineSpacing`, `--psm`, or a similar key in its config/ini file), lower the minimum detected gap so the engine splits lines that are closer together than the default. For Tesseract-based back-ends, also try `--psm 6` (uniform block) or `--psm 4` (single column) to influence how the layout analyst groups rows.

4. **Check font and export settings in the source document.** If the original document is generated (PDF, DOCX, etc.), increase the line spacing to at least 1.15× or add a small paragraph spacing before/after each line so the rendered gap is clearly visible.

5. **Update or swap the OCR engine/module** within the APT application if the above tuning still fails—newer engines (Tesseract 5, ABBYY Flexi, Windows OCR 4) handle tight lines better.

### Quick Diagnostic

Open the .TXT output and note *which* lines are merging. Open the same page in an image viewer and measure the pixel distance between baselines of the merged pair. If that distance is ≤ the engine's working resolution × (line height / 72), you are hitting the resolution/spacing threshold, and steps 1–3 will resolve it.

The fix is almost never a bug in the APT application's file-writing code; it is the OCR segmentation stage upstream. Increasing the inter-line gap—either in the source image or via engine parameters—will give the .TXT file one physical line per logical line.

When the gap between two physical lines in your source document is smaller than the engine's internal "line-break threshold" (typically a small fraction of the font size), the engine treats them as part of the same line and concatenates them in the output .TXT file.

### Most Common Causes in an APT Workflow

1. **Tight line spacing / small font in the source** – If the PDF or scanned image uses a font size where the leading is very close to the em-height, the vertical separation falls below the OCR line-break threshold.
2. **Low input resolution (DPI)** – At, say, 72 DPI the pixels representing the inter-line gap can be only 1–2 px, which many OCR engines (and the one bundled/called by APT) will treat as noise rather than a true line break.
3. **OCR "line merge" tolerance setting** – Many OCR engines expose a parameter (sometimes called *line-spacing factor*, *row merge distance*, or *minimum gap*) that controls how many font-heights of space must exist before a newline is emitted. The default in some APT profiles is generous, favoring fewer false line breaks at the cost of merging real ones.
4. **Page-orientation or crop-box mismatch** – If APT is feeding the OCR engine a rotated or mis-framed region, the engine's vertical-axis calculations are off, and it may not detect the expected line gaps.

### What You Can Do

- **Increase the source resolution.** Re-scan or re-export the source at 300 DPI or higher. This alone often resolves the merging because the pixel gap between lines becomes unambiguous.
- **Relax the OCR line-break threshold.** In the OCR engine's configuration (or the APT module that invokes it), look for a setting such as:
  - `LineSpacingFactor` / `RowGapThreshold`
  - `-t` or `--line-spacing` CLI flags
  - A property in the APT print/OCR profile (e.g., "Minimum line gap" or "Line merge distance")
  Lowering the required gap (or raising the sensitivity) will cause the engine to insert `\n` where it was previously merging.
- **Add explicit line spacing in the source.** If you control the document layout, increase the leading so the gap between baselines is at least ~1.3× the font size before sending it through OCR.
- **Post-process the .TXT.** If you cannot change the OCR settings, run a small post-processing step that inserts a newline at known delimiters (field boundaries, a fixed character count for a fixed-width report, or a regex pattern that matches the end-of-record marker APT writes).
- **Verify the APT OCR profile.** Some APT installations ship with a default OCR profile tuned for single-line headers. Switch to a "multiline" or "detailed" profile if one is available, or confirm the correct profile is selected for your detail-line report.

### Quick Diagnostic

Run the OCR engine in "debug/box" mode (output the bounding box of every detected word). In the resulting box list, check whether two logical lines are being assigned **two separate y-coordinates** or the **same y-coordinate**. If they share a y-coordinate, the merge is happening at the segmentation stage, and the threshold/resolution fixes above are what you need. If they already have distinct y-coordinates but the `.TXT` still shows them on one line, the issue is in the **text-serialization layer** (a missing `\n` in the export code), and you should look at APT's output-formatting template rather than the OCR engine itself.

## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines Into One

OCR engines determine line boundaries by detecting **vertical gaps** between rows of characters. When those gaps fall below the engine's configured **minimum line-separation threshold**, the engine classifies the adjacent rows as a single line and concatenates them in the output with no newline delimiter. In your APT application's .TXT export, you are seeing exactly that: the OCR pass occurred at the image/PDF level, and the merged results were written verbatim to the text file.

### Common Root Causes

1. **Tight line spacing in the source document.** If the original document (scanned page, rendered PDF, or generated report) has a leading of, say, 10 pt with 12 pt fonts, the vertical whitespace between baselines may be only 2 pt. Many OCR engines default to a 3–5 px (or ~3–4 pt) line-gap threshold, so those two rows are treated as one line.

2. **OCR engine "line-height" or "fixed-height" mode.** If the engine was configured for fixed-height characters with a height smaller than the actual glyph height (or the line pitch), it will pack multiple visual rows into a single logical line.

3. **No explicit line-break hints.** Plain OCR (unlike layout-aware OCR) has no structural model of paragraphs or table rows; it relies purely on spatial clustering. Without a clear enough gap, clustering merges rows.

4. **Downstream APT export step.** Some APT frameworks re-flow OCR'd text into fixed-width or CSV columns before writing the .TXT file, and a missing `\n` in the OCR output means the writer simply appends the next "line" on the same row.

### What You Can Do

| Lever | Action |
|---|---|
| **Increase line-gap threshold** | In your OCR configuration (e.g., Tesseract `--psm` / `Tesseract.mergeLineGap`, ABBYY `Lines.GapThreshold`, or the APT OCR module's equivalent "line spacing sensitivity" parameter), raise the minimum gap so closer rows are still split. |

| **Adjust source rendering** | If you control the upstream document, increase the font leading / line-height by 20–30 % so the OCR engine sees a clear inter-line gap. |
| **Post-process the .TXT** | Add a small transformation in the APT export step: scan the OCR output for patterns where two logical entries have been fused (e.g., a known delimiter, a tab, or a field-length overflow) and insert `\n` (or `\r\n`) at that boundary. |

## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines into One

**Root cause:** OCR engines detect line breaks by measuring the vertical pixel distance between the baselines (or top/bottom edges) of adjacent text rows. When that inter-line gap falls below the engine's internal **line-break threshold**, it classifies both rows as belonging to the same text line and concatenates them into a single output line in your `.TXT` file. Tight leading (e.g., 1.0× line spacing), low scan resolution, or small font sizes all shrink that gap and trigger the merge.

### Practical fixes (from most to least impactful)

1. **Increase inter-line spacing in the source document before capture.**
   - Set line spacing to at least **1.2–1.5×** in the document editor.
   - If you're scanning paper, make sure the original print isn't using single-spaced or condensed leading.

2. **Raise the capture/scan resolution.**
   - Scan at **300 dpi minimum** (600 dpi for small text). At 150 dpi the vertical gap between lines can be only 2–3 pixels, which is below most engines' break threshold.

3. **Adjust the OCR engine's line-detection / page-segmentation settings.**
   - **Tesseract:** Try `--psm 4` (assume a single column of variable-size text) or `--psm 6` (assume a uniform block). You can also edit the `configs/` files or use `tesseract` with `preserve_interword_spaces` to reduce unwanted merging.
   - **ABBYY / ABBYY FineReader:** In *Recognition → Layout*, increase the "line gap" or adjust the "line height tolerance."
   - **Microsoft / Windows OCR:** In the recognition profile, reduce the "line spacing sensitivity."
   - **Within your APT application:** Look for an OCR settings panel (often under *Preferences → OCR* or *Document Processing → Line Detection*). There is typically a **line-height tolerance** or **minimum vertical gap (px/pt)** slider—lowering it makes the engine more aggressive about inserting a newline.

4. **Post-process the `.TXT` file if you can't change the capture pipeline.**
   A quick script can re-split merged lines using known delimiters (tabs, repeated spaces, or capitalization of the next word):

   ```python
   import re
   text = open("output.txt").read()
   # Split where a space is immediately followed by a capital letter
   # (adjust the pattern to your document's conventions)

   ```

If that gap is **< ~8–10 px at 300 dpi**, most OCR engines will merge the lines. Increasing spacing or resolution to push that gap above the threshold resolves the issue directly.

When the OCR processes a source image or rendered layout and the inter-line spacing falls below its configured **line-separation threshold**, it collapses those rows into a single text line. In an APT application pipeline this typically stems from one (or a combination) of the following:

- **Block/zone detection misconfiguration.** If the APT OCR module is set to treat a region as a single "paragraph block" rather than recognizing individual lines, it will emit the text as one continuous string separated only by spaces.

2. **Increase the vertical pitch of the source lines.** If you control the layout that feeds the OCR (report definition, form template, print job), add a few points of leading between detail lines so the white-space band exceeds the OCR's minimum-gap requirement. 6. **Check for a known patch/bulletin.** If this is an Oracle/enterprise APT module, search the application's MOS/Support portal for the exact symptom "OCR merges lines" or "multiple lines on single line in TXT output." ## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines onto One Line

In your APT application, the OCR engine is failing to detect the vertical separation between text lines, so it treats adjacent baselines as a single logical line before writing to the .TXT output. This is a **line-segmentation** problem, not a character-recognition problem.

### Root Causes

- **Insufficient source resolution:** If the scanned/image source is below ~300 DPI (and especially below 200 DPI), the pixel gap between two lines is too small for the OCR's line-detection algorithm to register a break.
- **Tight leading / spacing:** If the document was exported or printed with minimal line spacing (e.g., single-spaced 10-point text), the vertical white space between lines falls below the OCR engine's minimum gap threshold.
- **Low contrast:** Light gray text or a slightly faded scan can cause the engine's projection-profile algorithm to read the rows of two lines as one continuous "ink band."
- **Engine default thresholds:** Many OCR libraries (Tesseract, ABBYY, A pengurus OCR module embedded in the APT app, etc.) use a default *minimum line gap* (often 2–3 pixels at the working resolution). If the actual gap is smaller, the lines are merged.

### What You Can Do (in order of least to most invasive)

1. **Raise the input image resolution.** Re-scan or re-export the source at 300–600 DPI. If the APT app accepts a file parameter for DPI, set it explicitly.

2. **Pre-process the image before OCR.** Apply a slight vertical stretch (e.g., 10–15 %) or a contrast/threshold pass so the inter-line white space is unambiguous. Most APT environments let you hook a pre-processing step (ImageMagick, OpenCV, or the app's own image filter).

3. **Adjust the OCR line-gap or line-height parameter.** If the APT application exposes OCR configuration (often a property like `minLineGap`, `lineSpacing`, `--psm`, or a similar key in its config/ini file), lower the minimum detected gap so the engine splits lines that are closer together than the default. For Tesseract-based back-ends, also try `--psm 6` (uniform block) or `--psm 4` (single column) to influence how the layout analyst groups rows.

4. **Check font and export settings in the source document.** If the original document is generated (PDF, DOCX, etc.), increase the line spacing to at least 1.15× or add a small paragraph spacing before/after each line so the rendered gap is clearly visible.

5. **Update or swap the OCR engine/module** within the APT application if the above tuning still fails—newer engines (Tesseract 5, ABBYY Flexi, Windows OCR 4) handle tight lines better.

### Quick Diagnostic

Open the .TXT output and note *which* lines are merging. Open the same page in an image viewer and measure the pixel distance between baselines of the merged pair. If that distance is ≤ the engine's working resolution × (line height / 72), you are hitting the resolution/spacing threshold, and steps 1–3 will resolve it.

The fix is almost never a bug in the APT application's file-writing code; it is the OCR segmentation stage upstream. Increasing the inter-line gap—either in the source image or via engine parameters—will give the .TXT file one physical line per logical line.

2. **Image / PDF resolution**
   - Ensure the input document is scanned or rendered at **300 dpi or higher**. At 72 dpi a 12-pt font with single spacing may only produce a 2–3 px gap, which most engines won't split. Re-import the source at a higher resolution and re-run OCR.

3. **Source document formatting**
   - If you control the layout before OCR, increase the line spacing (e.g., from single to 1.15× or 1.5×) or add a small vertical gap between detail-line groups. This gives the OCR engine a clearer cue.

4. **Post-processing in the APT pipeline**
   - Verify that the APT application's own text-extraction step is not **stripping carriage returns** or collapsing whitespace after the OCR step. If the APT writer is responsible, look for a "preserve line breaks" or "raw output" flag in its configuration.

5. **OCR engine-specific settings**
   - If you can select or tune the underlying engine (e.g., Tesseract, ABBYY, ABB FineReader, or an in-house engine), raise the `--psm` (Page Segmentation Mode) setting or enable *column/line detection* explicitly. In your APT application's .TXT export, you are seeing exactly that: the OCR pass occurred at the image/PDF level, and the merged results were written verbatim to the text file.

### Common Root Causes

1. **Tight line spacing in the source document.** If the original document (scanned page, rendered PDF, or generated report) has a leading of, say, 10 pt with 12 pt fonts, the vertical whitespace between baselines may be only 2 pt. Many OCR engines default to a 3–5 px (or ~3–4 pt) line-gap threshold, so those two rows are treated as one line.

2. **OCR engine "line-height" or "fixed-height" mode.** If the engine was configured for fixed-height characters with a height smaller than the actual glyph height (or the line pitch), it will pack multiple visual rows into a single logical line.

3. **No explicit line-break hints.** Plain OCR (unlike layout-aware OCR) has no structural model of paragraphs or table rows; it relies purely on spatial clustering. Without a clear enough gap, clustering merges rows.

### Practical fixes (from most to least impactful)

1. **Increase inter-line spacing in the source document before capture.**

   - If you're scanning paper, make sure the original print isn't using single-spaced or condensed leading.

2. **Raise the capture/scan resolution.**
   - Scan at **300 dpi minimum** (600 dpi for small text). At 150 dpi the vertical gap between lines can be only 2–3 pixels, which is below most engines' break threshold.

3. **Adjust the OCR engine's line-detection / page-segmentation settings.**
   - **Tesseract:** Try `--psm 4` (assume a single column of variable-size text) or `--psm 6` (assume a uniform block). You can also edit the `configs/` files or use `tesseract` with `preserve_interword_spaces` to reduce unwanted merging.
   - **ABBYY / ABBYY FineReader:** In *Recognition → Layout*, increase the "line gap" or adjust the "line height tolerance."
   - **Microsoft / Windows OCR:** In the recognition profile, reduce the "line spacing sensitivity."
   - **Within your APT application:** Look for an OCR settings panel (often under *Preferences → OCR* or *Document Processing → Line Detection*). There is typically a **line-height tolerance** or **minimum vertical gap (px/pt)** slider—lowering it makes the engine more aggressive about inserting a newline.

4. **Post-process the `.TXT` file if you can't change the capture pipeline.**
   A quick script can re-split merged lines using known delimiters (tabs, repeated spaces, or capitalization of the next word):

   ```python
   import re
   text = open("output.txt").read()
   # Split where a space is immediately followed by a capital letter
   # (adjust the pattern to your document's conventions)
   fixed = re.sub(r' (?=[A-Z][a-z])', '\n', text)
   open("output_fixed.txt", "w").write(fixed)
   ```

5. **Check for font/rendering artifacts.**
   Some OCR engines mis-interpret descenders (g, p, y) or ascenders (h, k, l) as bridging two lines, preventing a break. Using a clean, sans-serif font at 10 pt or larger in the source helps.

### Quick diagnostic

Open the source image in an image editor and measure the vertical pixel distance between the bottom of one text row and the top of the next. If that gap is **< ~8–10 px at 300 dpi**, most OCR engines will merge the lines. Increasing spacing or resolution to push that gap above the threshold resolves the issue directly.

## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines onto One Line

In your APT application, the OCR engine is failing to detect the vertical separation between text lines, so it treats adjacent baselines as a single logical line before writing to the .TXT output. This is a **line-segmentation** problem, not a character-recognition problem.

### Root Causes

- **Insufficient source resolution:** If the scanned/image source is below ~300 DPI (and especially below 200 DPI), the pixel gap between two lines is too small for the OCR's line-detection algorithm to register a break.
- **Tight leading / spacing:** If the document was exported or printed with minimal line spacing (e.g., single-spaced 10-point text), the vertical white space between lines falls below the OCR engine's minimum gap threshold.
- **Low contrast:** Light gray text or a slightly faded scan can cause the engine's projection-profile algorithm to read the rows of two lines as one continuous "ink band."
- **Engine default thresholds:** Many OCR libraries (Tesseract, ABBYY, A pengurus OCR module embedded in the APT app, etc.) use a default *minimum line gap* (often 2–3 pixels at the working resolution). If the actual gap is smaller, the lines are merged.

### What You Can Do (in order of least to most invasive)

1. **Raise the input image resolution.** Re-scan or re-export the source at 300–600 DPI. If the APT app accepts a file parameter for DPI, set it explicitly.

2. **Pre-process the image before OCR.** Apply a slight vertical stretch (e.g., 10–15 %) or a contrast/threshold pass so the inter-line white space is unambiguous. Most APT environments let you hook a pre-processing step (ImageMagick, OpenCV, or the app's own image filter).

3. **Adjust the OCR line-gap or line-height parameter.** If the APT application exposes OCR configuration (often a property like `minLineGap`, `lineSpacing`, `--psm`, or a similar key in its config/ini file), lower the minimum detected gap so the engine splits lines that are closer together than the default. For Tesseract-based back-ends, also try `--psm 6` (uniform block) or `--psm 4` (single column) to influence how the layout analyst groups rows.

4. **Check font and export settings in the source document.** If the original document is generated (PDF, DOCX, etc.), increase the line spacing to at least 1.15× or add a small paragraph spacing before/after each line so the rendered gap is clearly visible.

5. **Update or swap the OCR engine/module** within the APT application if the above tuning still fails—newer engines (Tesseract 5, ABBYY Flexi, Windows OCR 4) handle tight lines better.

### Quick Diagnostic

Open the .TXT output and note *which* lines are merging. Open the same page in an image viewer and measure the pixel distance between baselines of the merged pair. If that distance is ≤ the engine's working resolution × (line height / 72), you are hitting the resolution/spacing threshold, and steps 1–3 will resolve it.

The fix is almost never a bug in the APT application's file-writing code; it is the OCR segmentation stage upstream. Increasing the inter-line gap—either in the source image or via engine parameters—will give the .TXT file one physical line per logical line.

**Root cause:** OCR engines detect line breaks by measuring the vertical pixel distance between the baselines (or top/bottom edges) of adjacent text rows. When that inter-line gap falls below the engine's internal **line-break threshold**, it classifies both rows as belonging to the same text line and concatenates them into a single output line in your `.TXT` file. Tight leading (e.g., 1.0× line spacing), low scan resolution, or small font sizes all shrink that gap and trigger the merge.

### Practical fixes (from most to least impactful)

1. **Increase inter-line spacing in the source document before capture.**
   - Set line spacing to at least **1.2–1.5×** in the document editor.
   - If you're scanning paper, make sure the original print isn't using single-spaced or condensed leading.

2. **Raise the capture/scan resolution.**
   - Scan at **300 dpi minimum** (600 dpi for small text). At 150 dpi the vertical gap between lines can be only 2–3 pixels, which is below most engines' break threshold.

3. **Adjust the OCR engine's line-detection / page-segmentation settings.**
   - **Tesseract:** Try `--psm 4` (assume a single column of variable-size text) or `--psm 6` (assume a uniform block). You can also edit the `configs/` files or use `tesseract` with `preserve_interword_spaces` to reduce unwanted merging.
   - **ABBYY / ABBYY FineReader:** In *Recognition → Layout*, increase the "line gap" or adjust the "line height tolerance."
   - **Microsoft / Windows OCR:** In the recognition profile, reduce the "line spacing sensitivity."
   - **Within your APT application:** Look for an OCR settings panel (often under *Preferences → OCR* or *Document Processing → Line Detection*). There is typically a **line-height tolerance** or **minimum vertical gap (px/pt)** slider—lowering it makes the engine more aggressive about inserting a newline.

4. **Post-process the `.TXT` file if you can't change the capture pipeline.**
   A quick script can re-split merged lines using known delimiters (tabs, repeated spaces, or capitalization of the next word):

   ```python
   import re
   text = open("output.txt").read()
   # Split where a space is immediately followed by a capital letter
   # (adjust the pattern to your document's conventions)

   ```

5. **Check for font/rendering artifacts.**
   Some OCR engines mis-interpret descenders (g, p, y) or ascenders (h, k, l) as bridging two lines, preventing a break. Using a clean, sans-serif font at 10 pt or larger in the source helps.

Open the source image in an image editor and measure the vertical pixel distance between the bottom of one text row and the top of the next. If that gap is **< ~8–10 px at 300 dpi**, most OCR engines will merge the lines. Increasing spacing or resolution to push that gap above the threshold resolves the issue directly.

## Why This Happens

OCR engines detect line breaks primarily by looking for a **vertical gap (whitespace band)** between rows of glyphs. When the OCR processes a source image or rendered layout and the inter-line spacing falls below its configured **line-separation threshold**, it collapses those rows into a single text line. In an APT application pipeline this typically stems from one (or a combination) of the following:

- **Tight leading / small vertical pitch** in the source document. If the detail lines are rendered (or scanned) with a line pitch that is less than the OCR engine's minimum blank-line height, the bounding boxes of adjacent lines overlap vertically and are treated as one line.
- **Low scan/capture resolution or poor contrast.** At lower DPI the descenders and ascenders of adjacent lines bleed into the white space, preventing the engine from finding a clean horizontal clear band.
- **Block/zone detection misconfiguration.** If the APT OCR module is set to treat a region as a single "paragraph block" rather than recognizing individual lines, it will emit the text as one continuous string separated only by spaces.
- **Missing or stripped carriage-return / line-feed characters** in the intermediate format (e.g., the OCR writes a single `<line>` element or a flat character stream) before the APT layer flushes the `.TXT` output.

## What You Can Do

1. **Adjust the line-separation / line-break sensitivity parameter.** In the APT application's OCR configuration (often under *Processing Options*, *OCR Settings*, or a properties/parameters table for the OCR step), look for a setting such as:
   - `LINE_SPACING_THRESHOLD` or `MIN_LINE_GAP` (in pixels or points)
   - `PARAGRAPH_DETECTION` = ON/OFF

   Lowering the threshold so the engine flags smaller vertical gaps as new lines is the most direct fix.

2. **Increase the vertical pitch of the source lines.** If you control the layout that feeds the OCR (report definition, form template, print job), add a few points of leading between detail lines so the white-space band exceeds the OCR's minimum-gap requirement. Even 2–3 pt extra line spacing is often enough.

3. **Raise the capture/scan resolution.** Rescan or re-render at **300 DPI or higher** and ensure high black-on-white contrast. This gives the engine more pixels to work with when searching for the horizontal clear band.

4. **Change the OCR post-processing / output mode.** Some APT OCR configurations have an option for:
   - *Layout* vs. *Reading Order* output
   - Whether to preserve physical line breaks or flow text into paragraphs

5. **Post-process the `.TXT` file programmatically.** If the APT OCR parameters cannot be changed, a simple script (awk, Python, or a database SQL `REPLACE`/`REGEXP_SUBSTR` pass) can split the merged line at known field boundaries, column positions, or delimiters that separate the detail-line values.

6. **Check for a known patch/bulletin.** If this is an Oracle/enterprise APT module, search the application's MOS/Support portal for the exact symptom "OCR merges lines" or "multiple lines on single line in TXT output." Vendor-supplied patches or profile-option fixes are common for this class of OCR bounding-box bug.

Open the OCR intermediate output (often a ZIP, TSV, or annotated image the APT step produces before writing the final `.TXT`). If the intermediate already shows the lines merged, the problem is in the **engine/configuration** (items 1–3). ## Why OCR Merges Multiple Lines onto One Line

In your APT application, the OCR engine is failing to detect the vertical separation between text lines, so it treats adjacent baselines as a single logical line before writing to the .TXT output. This is a **line-segmentation** problem, not a character-recognition problem.

### Root Causes

- **Insufficient source resolution:** If the scanned/image source is below ~300 DPI (and especially below 200 DPI), the pixel gap between two lines is too small for the OCR's line-detection algorithm to register a break.
- **Tight leading / spacing:** If the document was exported or printed with minimal line spacing (e.g., single-spaced 10-point text), the vertical white space between lines falls below the OCR engine's minimum gap threshold.
- **Low contrast:** Light gray text or a slightly faded scan can cause the engine's projection-profile algorithm to read the rows of two lines as one continuous "ink band."
- **Engine default thresholds:** Many OCR libraries (Tesseract, ABBYY, A pengurus OCR module embedded in the APT app, etc.) use a default *minimum line gap* (often 2–3 pixels at the working resolution). If the actual gap is smaller, the lines are merged.

### What You Can Do (in order of least to most invasive)

1. **Raise the input image resolution.** Re-scan or re-export the source at 300–600 DPI. If the APT app accepts a file parameter for DPI, set it explicitly.

2. **Pre-process the image before OCR.** Apply a slight vertical stretch (e.g., 10–15 %) or a contrast/threshold pass so the inter-line white space is unambiguous. Most APT environments let you hook a pre-processing step (ImageMagick, OpenCV, or the app's own image filter).

3. **Adjust the OCR line-gap or line-height parameter.** If the APT application exposes OCR configuration (often a property like `minLineGap`, `lineSpacing`, `--psm`, or a similar key in its config/ini file), lower the minimum detected gap so the engine splits lines that are closer together than the default. For Tesseract-based back-ends, also try `--psm 6` (uniform block) or `--psm 4` (single column) to influence how the layout analyst groups rows.

4. **Check font and export settings in the source document.** If the original document is generated (PDF, DOCX, etc.), increase the line spacing to at least 1.15× or add a small paragraph spacing before/after each line so the rendered gap is clearly visible.

5. **Update or swap the OCR engine/module** within the APT application if the above tuning still fails—newer engines (Tesseract 5, ABBYY Flexi, Windows OCR 4) handle tight lines better.

### Quick Diagnostic

Open the .TXT output and note *which* lines are merging. Open the same page in an image viewer and measure the pixel distance between baselines of the merged pair. If that distance is ≤ the engine's working resolution × (line height / 72), you are hitting the resolution/spacing threshold, and steps 1–3 will resolve it.

The fix is almost never a bug in the APT application's file-writing code; it is the OCR segmentation stage upstream. Increasing the inter-line gap—either in the source image or via engine parameters—will give the .TXT file one physical line per logical line.

## Why OCR Is Merging Multiple Lines onto a Single Line

This is a common OCR line-separation problem, typically caused by the OCR engine's **line-detection threshold** not being satisfied relative to the vertical spacing in your source document. Here's what is happening and how to address it:

### Root Cause

OCR engines determine line boundaries by detecting a minimum **vertical pixel gap** between rows of glyphs. When the spacing between your "detail lines" falls below that threshold (often due to tight line-spacing, small fonts, or low scan resolution), the engine treats them as one continuous line and writes a single \n (or none) into the .TXT output.

### What to Check / Fix in the APT Application and OCR Layer

1. **OCR line-height / line-tolerance parameter**
   - In the OCR profile (or the OCR settings exposed by the APT application), look for a parameter such as *line gap*, *line height tolerance*, or *minimum inter-line spacing* (typically expressed in pixels or points). Lower this value so the engine recognises tighter gaps as line breaks.

2. **Image / PDF resolution**
   - Ensure the input document is scanned or rendered at **300 dpi or higher**. At 72 dpi a 12-pt font with single spacing may only produce a 2–3 px gap, which most engines won't split. Re-import the source at a higher resolution and re-run OCR.

3. **Source document formatting**
   - If you control the layout before OCR, increase the line spacing (e.g., from single to 1.15× or 1.5×) or add a small vertical gap between detail-line groups. This gives the OCR engine a clearer cue.

4. **Post-processing in the APT pipeline**
   - Verify that the APT application's own text-extraction step is not **stripping carriage returns** or collapsing whitespace after the OCR step. Inspect the raw OCR output (before the APT formatting stage) to confirm whether the merge happens at the OCR layer or during the application's .TXT writer. If the APT writer is responsible, look for a "preserve line breaks" or "raw output" flag in its configuration.

5. **OCR engine-specific settings**
   - If you can select or tune the underlying engine (e.g., Tesseract, ABBYY, ABB FineReader, or an in-house engine), raise the `--psm` (Page Segmentation Mode) setting or enable *column/line detection* explicitly. For Tesseract, for example, `-psm 4` (assume single column) or `-psm 6` (assume uniform block) often separates lines better than the default auto mode.

### Quick Diagnostic

- Run OCR on a small test page with 3–4 known detail lines spaced at different gaps (e.g., 6 pt, 10 pt, 14 pt).
- Note the minimum gap at which the engine correctly emits a newline. That number tells you the exact threshold to adjust in your OCR profile.
- Confirm in the APT application's log or debug output whether the newline characters are present after OCR but removed during .TXT assembly.

### TL;DR

The merger is almost always a **line-spacing-threshold vs. actual-gap** mismatch. Increase the vertical spacing in the source (or resolution), lower the OCR engine's minimum line-gap setting, and verify the APT application isn't collapsing newlines in its own text-assembly step.

Missing Line-Terminator Characters (Most Likely) The APT application's OCR-to-text writer is not inserting carriage return (`\r`) / line feed (`\n`) characters between the text rows it extracted. Open the `.TXT` file in a **hex editor** (e.g., HxD, 010 Editor). If you see a continuous stream of printable characters with no `0D 0A` (Windows) or `0A` (Unix) bytes between what should be separate detail lines, the writer is simply not emitting line breaks. **Fix:** Look in the APT application's **export / output settings** for an option such as: - *"Preserve line breaks"* - *"Maintain physical layout"* - *"Insert CR/LF between lines"* - *"Multi-line output"* (vs. a single-line/flat mode) ### 2. OCR Line-Segmentation Threshold Too Lenient The OCR engine groups text into "rows" based on a **vertical pixel/pt gap threshold**. Export Template / Format Not Preserving Rows Some APT applications use a **report template** (e.g., an XML, DXML, or print-driver mapping) to lay out OCR results. `, a paragraph tag, or a CR character) after each iteration. ### Quick Diagnostic Checklist | Check | How | |---|---| | Are `0D 0A` bytes actually in the file? | Hex-editor the `.TXT` | | Does the APT output log mention "single-line mode"? | Review the processing/export log | | Do other documents with wider line spacing work correctly? | Test a document with ≥ 10 pt line spacing | | Is there an OCR confidence / margin setting? | Lower the min-gap threshold | ### Summary The lines are not being "lost" by OCR; they are being **extracted correctly but written without line terminators**, or the **line-segmentation threshold** is merging physically separate rows before export.
